NO. 050 · Songbirds & City Birds / Leiothrichidae · Laughingthrushes

Chinese Hwamei

画眉 · huà méi Garrulax canorus
Resident Uncommon 21–24 cm Protected (Class II) IUCN LC

China's most famous cage bird — and now a protected species

A white ring around the eye trails back into a long eyebrow stripe, as if it had been painted on — hence the name, 'painted eyebrow'. Its song is reckoned among the finest of any Chinese bird, and for that very reason it was once trapped in huge numbers; it is now a nationally protected species (Class II).

Gallery

One scientific illustration for shape and colour blocks, two field photographs for how it looks in real light. Click any image to enlarge.

Identification

  • EyebrowWhite around the eye, extending back into a fine white supercilium that droops slightly at the rear — the most characteristic feature of the species.
  • PlumageUpperparts brown, crown and back with dark streaks, underparts yellowish-brown with faint streaks across breast and belly.
  • BillYellowish-brown, slightly downcurved, stout and strong — made for turning over leaf litter.
  • ShapeMedium-sized and roundish, tail fairly long, usually progressing over the ground in hops.

Behaviour

A bird of the understorey, turning over fallen leaves for insects, earthworms and fruit; secretive in habit but giving its position away by voice. Wary, and when disturbed it slips low into dense cover. A resident in South China, in hill forest, bamboo and gully thickets. Wild numbers have declined markedly through decades of trapping for the cage-bird trade.

Voice

An extraordinarily varied song, wide in range and often described as coloratura — clear whistles, trills and mimicry interwoven at a free rhythm. One of the most recognisable dawn songs in South China's hills.

Where to find it in Zhuhai

  • Banzhang Hill understorey
  • Fenghuang Hill ravines
  • hill-edge scrub in Doumen
  • Qi'ao Island forest edges
Field note
A nationally protected species (Class II); capture and trade are prohibited. Please do not use playback to draw birds in — disturbance during the breeding season directly reduces their success.
